title: The forty as a life
hookLine: intention, the pillars, the heart, the tongue, mercy: al-Nawawi's forty, read first to last, run like one life
tomorrow: you've read all forty. could you say even one without your phone?

cards: The lights go down in the gym and the senior slideshow starts. A toddler in a birthday crown, a missing front tooth, a science fair volcano, a prom photo. Nobody in the room sees a stack of pictures.
They see one life, in order. Now run al-Nawawi's forty-two hadith like that slideshow, first to last. It opens on intention.
It closes on a voice saying: as long as you call. So what happens in between, and why does a book of foundations end on someone who has failed?

teach.b: Watch the order. Frame one: actions are by intentions. Before anything, why.
Then a stranger in white sits knee to knee with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and lays out the map of the religion, ending with worship Allah as if you see Him.

teach.h: THE MAP, THE PILLARS, THE HEART.
teach.b: Then the pillars, the frame of the house. Then the inside: a lump of flesh in the body that, when it's sound, keeps the whole body sound. The heart.
Then the tongue: speak good or be silent. Then other people, everywhere: love for your brother what you love for yourself, relieve a distress, no harm.
Near the end, a traveler: be in the world as a stranger, or someone passing through. And the last frame isn't a trophy.
It's a sacred hadith in Tirmidhi's collection, in paraphrase: as long as you call on Me and hope in Me, I forgive you, and I don't mind. That's the answer.
A life built on the first forty-one still slips, so the book leaves the door open.

Al-Nawawi never says he arranged it as a life; that's one way to read his order. But here's a thing to tell a friend tonight: the collection that starts with why you do things ends with what to do when you didn't.

how: Muslims who study al-Nawawi's forty often go back over the whole set when they finish, choosing a few to keep close; teachers commonly review it from the first hadith to the last.

games.q: what does “the forty as a life” mean?
o: al-Nawawi's hadith read in order, like one life
the forty days a new Muslim studies before praying
a rule to read one hadith a year for forty years

games.q: the forty, first to last — tap the pairs.

s: the forty end on a reward list for the best believers
the last hadith is about someone who has failed and calls; the door stays open.
hadith one: actions are by intentions.
al-Nawawi wrote that he arranged the forty as the story of a life
he never says so; reading the order as a life is one way to see it.

games.q: you finished all forty-two and feel like a fraud: you know them, and you still snapped at your sister today. what does the last hadith say?
o: close the book; knowing them without living them is pointless.
the collection ends on calling and being forgiven; come back and keep going.
intention is what counts, so the snapping doesn't really matter.
games.why: the book of foundations ends with a door left open: as long as you call on Me and hope in Me, I forgive you.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write by hand the three of the forty-two you'd keep if you could keep only three. Short names are fine: intention, the heart, as long as you call.
For the sit, look at the three together and notice what kind of day they'd make.

wordCard.voice: The forty as a life: al-Nawawi's hadith read first to last, intention at the start and a door left open at the end.

orig.note: Arabic: forty. the collection is known as al-Arba'in, the forty, though it holds forty-two.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: a life in forty, the why at the start and the door still open at the end. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in al-Nawawiyyah, hadith 1, 2, 3, 6, 13, 15, 32, 36, 40, 42 (intention; the stranger in white; built on five; the lump of flesh; love for your brother; speak good or be silent; no harm; relieve a distress; a stranger or a traveler; as long as you call)
Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3540 (Anas: O son of Adam, as long as you call on Me and hope in Me, I forgive you, and I don't mind)
